text:
Nvidia, the company famed for supplying the picks and shovels that are powering the current AI boom, has its sights set on healthcare. The big tech firm provides the infrastructure — chips and software — underpinning the technology used in the sector.

Its chief executive Jensen Huang has previously predicted that half of the big pharmaceutical companies’ research and development budgets will shift from traditional labs to AI-driven projects.

As vice-president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell is responsible for selling Nvidia’s hardware and software platforms that support medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery and healthcare analytics. Powell joined the company in 2008 and helped to establish its GPU computing chips as a platform for medical imaging instruments.

In this conversation with the FT’s technology correspondent, Cristina Criddle, she argues that AI can help ease the workload on doctors, address the global shortage of trained medical staff, improve patient care and accelerate research into diseases and drug development.

Cristina Criddle: What do you think the hospital of the future is going to look like?

Kimberly Powell: I think we’re actually starting to experience it now. A recent publication by Menlo Ventures found that the healthcare services industry is deploying AI almost three times faster than any other part of the economy in the US. And it’s a telling sign. It’s essentially a trend the world’s never seen before because healthcare is generally a bit technology-averse, for good reason. They need to make sure there’s safety built in and all of these things.

But there’s truly a global phenomenon going on where every nation around the globe is suffering from the demand for healthcare services far outstripping the supply of healthcare professionals.

The statistics in China, for example: they have an ageing population of 20mn per year, but they’re only birthing 7mn. And this is happening across the world, and so we have a huge opportunity.

Sometimes, nurses spend 40 per cent of their day on administrative work. A doctor’s day is filled with administrative work, so this is the point right now where AI is being deployed on hockey-stick trajectories. And so just like you asked if you could record this conversation, you’re going to walk into every doctor’s office, and they’re going to ask the same thing. For all the reasons you enjoy the service of transcription and potentially now using agents to summarise or format into different pieces that you’re going to write, similarly, you could deploy that for a whole bunch of health services. It could help the clinician pre-generate the report that he or she can go in and just check and balance after the fact, or it could help kick off another agent that might go schedule the next appointment.

CC: I’m not recording a medical conversation. I think a lot of patients and medical practitioners would be a bit hesitant to have this thing [my phone’s recording app] always on, listening in on a medical appointment. So how do you approach security issues when using AI in this setting?

KP: That’s why there are specific healthcare companies that are building the solution. Nvidia doesn’t provide these services. We provide a lot of the underlying technology so these services can get built. These are HIPAA-compliant [the US regulatory standards requiring medical records to be protected and allowing patients access to their data] application developers. They’re thoughtful of how long and what they store because you can parse the data and only take on the most valuable or necessary information to do that. There’s de-identification and anonymisation that can be deployed, and, again, this is AI in service of AI in many ways.

For the doctor, now that using this technology is as simple as a phone app, they can just hit a button. There’s no barrier to understanding how to use this technology. From the patient’s perspective, I think that, perhaps if there’s any apprehension, the doctor will be able to have this conversation with eye contact and physical feedback, whereas otherwise they would be looking away at a screen and typing.

It’s been very apparent for a decade or more now that we’ve lost our clinicians to typing

And it’s already been very apparent for a decade or more now that we’ve lost our clinicians to typing. And when they’re having to type for the conditions of data entry to make sure that reimbursement happens, you’re probably losing context. You’re definitely losing the personal connection. This is all in service of creating better patient outcomes, and when you can capture all the necessary information and maybe even just physically tune in . . . There’s so much good that will come of that.

So you’re reinventing the doctor experience and, actually, these companies that have invented these platforms will say it’s saved the doctors from leaving the profession because they were spending all of their night-time and weekends trying to catch up on all the paperwork, so they’re going to stay in the profession longer, which we need . . . because we’re already in a shortage.

CC: One of the issues there is that because everybody is so under pressure, systems are out of date, data is all over the place and not connected from hospital to hospital. For agents to really work well and for AI to really work well, it needs to be able to sift through that data.

KP: I think agents are overcoming a lot of it. I’m not saying it’s a solved problem yet, because some of it will be at the system level. Even as Nvidia, an enterprise, our data is all over the place and messy and the systems don’t speak [to each other]. But what agents are able to do is when they’re prompted with work, the reasoning aspect of these models now breaks it down piece by piece.

And once you understand what pieces are necessary, those interconnections exist. There are ways to get into the electronic health record . . . [and] ways of getting the lab work in. And so while they’re not [connected], the agent can actually get it together and synthesise it. These antiquated systems of record exist everywhere, but there’s this new agentic layer that can sit on top of it and get over all of that nastiness.

CC: And you’ll need to have hardware that can also run these agents, and so you’ll need to completely upgrade computer systems at each hospital, which won’t be cheap. How can hospitals try to budget for this when they’re already strapped for cash?

KP: Say that in order to meet my patient demand, I would have to potentially hire another 100 healthcare professionals. The problem with that is that there aren’t more nurses and doctors just hanging around, waiting to be hired. So we actually have a dilemma there.

But in order to serve that, what if you took that money and built it into the infrastructure that allowed you to essentially operate as if you had 100 more healthcare professionals? That’s why AI is coming right at the right time. And it’s nonsensical to think about it as any human job replacement because there just aren’t enough humans for the jobs. The only way we’re going to really close this huge demand-and-supply gap is through levels of AI and automation.

AI has now become ‘hireable’ in healthcare because of the agentic systems allowing them to have the appropriate knowledge, the appropriate guardrails, the domain specificity that this particular domain needs. There are ways to check and balance any kind of hallucination. And frankly, there are still humans in the loop . . . so it’s really about turbocharging humans by 10 or more times.

What if you took that money and built it into the infrastructure that allowed you to essentially operate as if you had 100 more healthcare professionals?

CC: How do you think that’s going to change training and experience? So, you take this budget that you have for staff, which you can’t find because there’s a shortage, you start using AI, and then younger or junior staff will come through using these systems, but they might not have as much hands-on experience because the agents are doing more of the role. How do you ensure that we’re still making sure that if all the systems shut down, if there was a power cut for whatever reason, this individual feels confident enough and independent enough to be able to do it themselves?

KP: I’m not a healthcare professional, but I also could maybe speak to it as an employee. It’s not like they don’t still go through their formal training and residency. What you are doing is you’re taking somebody who might be in their first few years of practice, and these tools are essentially up-levelling them to somebody who’s been in the practice 30 years. It’s really an uplift of the entire industry.

But it doesn’t remove the fact that experience and training still matter, and the people coming into the profession will be AI natives. They will be living now with ChatGPT in their pocket, and they’ll be even smarter than we were when we came out of school. That’s going to be obvious because the amount of information they can touch and use, even in their schooling and in their early days of practice, is going to be more than any human before them.

CC: Jensen’s prediction that half of pharma R&D spending would be shifted towards generating intelligence. I wonder if you could elaborate on that a bit and let me know the timeframes, too?

KP: If you think about the historic way that science has been done. It is very much human research and physical laboratory experimentation. Oftentimes, it’s this process: I have an idea, I do some research, I form a hypothesis, I design an experiment, and then I run the experiment. And then I might take that information and go through it again. So it’s very human-limited, and it’s very physical lab-limited. I haven’t described any computation in that flow.

I’ll use drug discovery and R&D as an anchoring point because we do a lot of work in this area. The industry itself takes, at best, about 10 years to get a drug to market. It costs over $2bn to do that. And frankly, they still have a 90 per cent failure rate. So it’s not a good situation.

What could help this is if we have three things that could improve. One, an understanding of biology in the first place. Two, we need to design a molecule. And then the third thing we need to do is optimise that molecule so that it has the best characteristics for treating a disease. And ideally, in the future, to treat your personal disease. Not our collective thing that’s called ovarian cancer, but your particular ovarian cancer.

CC: There are so many exciting start-ups I talk to in this space, and then you have Google DeepMind, you have Isomorphic Labs [the drug discovery start-up spun out of DeepMind in 2021], but we’re still yet to see a drug to market. How long do you think that will take, and how much of that is the process after finding this molecule, including the clinical trials?

KP: It has [a role] to play, but when Jensen said 50 per cent, let’s recognise that now that we can represent the world of drugs in a computer, that understands design and optimises, we’re going to turbocharge that by 100x. It is the case now in certain areas that the designing of molecules in silico [research that is solely performed using software and digital modelling] is so good that it’s becoming almost described as a solved problem. Almost, right?

And that’s come in a very few short years. The optimisation problem is now where you start to bring in things like computational simulation, and we’re working on that, like how do we make sure that these molecules aren’t toxic to humans? There’s the other part of understanding biology, which is still a huge endeavour. And when you can understand biology better, and you can simulate more, not only are we now able to design the molecule much faster, but we’ll be able to use that to run simulations of what this would look like in a patient, which will facilitate the next part, which is clinical development.

We’ll have much more insight: 90 per cent of drugs fail in that first phase of clinical development, but with more and more of this understanding of biology in silico and being able to optimise these molecules, we’re going to start to improve that failure rate. I cannot tell you when that’s going to happen, but let’s all understand that the amount of progress we’ve had in the last 24 months is something we could have never predicted.

CC: I’ve just done this podcast about humans and emotional interactions with AI. And one of the areas we looked at was the care sector, where, in South Korea, there are dolls with built-in chatbots. But they’re also taking the transcript. They will do a code red if this person is very isolated or feeling suicidal, and green for something positive. And the case study we had thought it was really positive, but at the same time, this person’s care worker said, ‘it’s a lot of extra admin for me to go through these logs and to check all of this.’ And so you have this parallel problem, which you highlighted earlier: there just aren’t enough people in these roles to do what they want. So how do you make sure that you’re not adding labour and taking away the parts of the job that they like, which is the human touch?

KP: With every AI system, the more it gets used and experienced, the [more] opportunity you have to improve it. If you remember using ChatGPT at the beginning, it threw a lot of BS your way. But now, if you’re using the new LLMs, they’re pretty exquisite. They’re pretty accurate. They’re showing you the evidence. That’s all going to be built into these systems. It just takes a little time because it’s happening so fast. And so that system is going to self-improve. And so long as the experience is OK, we have to trust that technology’s going to solve the bit of extra work that it takes.

And so we should get comfortable with that. We’re not going to have a generic system for every doctor. We’re going to have Dr Powell’s version of every agent because it’s going to talk like me. It’s going to think like me . . . So I think that is a solvable problem, but I appreciate how it did that for a long time in patient monitoring systems, too many false alarms, so it wasn’t helpful. But these systems have the ability to reduce the noise.

CC: So tell me about physical AI?

KP: On the physical AI front, there are two super important ways that this is going to be transformative. We want every hospital to be a robot, and what do I mean by that? Camera systems are just the eyes of the hospital. Being able to build spatial intelligence: what’s going on? Is my patient lost in the corridor? Is that too congested? Where is that ultrasound machine that I need down the hallway? All of this stuff that really hinders good flow and potentially causes a lot of unnecessary delay or deployment of human resources. So that’s a form of physical AI.

Next, imagine I say, ‘oh, well, the sheets are over here, but the bed that I need to be made is over there.’ Instead of a nurse having to transport sheets, couldn’t we deploy a delivery robot to do such a thing? And so now that you have your vision, you can understand what’s going on, you can action an embodied AI to now go off and navigate such a system.

And to me, that’s just like, why haven’t we done it yet, right? If Amazon warehouses can be that intelligent, smart and efficient, it’s sad that we wouldn’t put this level of tech in a hospital.

But then we’re going to go into robotic systems, either for surgery or to facilitate autonomous scanning of patients. Because the more we’re making the upfront understanding of what [we] need efficient, the more services we’re going to require downstream, the more operations we’re probably going to need, the more imaging . . . [This] is why we’re hiring more radiologists than we were before and [bear in mind] one of the godfathers [of AI, Geoffrey Hinton] thought this profession was maybe not going to be in existence [by] now. AI is actually increasing the demand for . . . radiologists.

With some level of physical automation, we’ve got to have both the digital world agents and the ability to deploy work in a physical environment and that will come in all forms of robotics, whether the building itself is a robot, delivery robots being very helpful, and then even clinical robots that can help deliver different things. So that’s just a super exciting world.

title: At Its First-Ever Cannes, OpenAI Says 'We Are Clearly In The Advertising Business Now'
description:

text:
OpenAI didn’t make its Cannes Lions debut from a Croisette rooftop or in a branded beach club.

Instead, the company summoned a small group of reporters late Monday morning to a semi-secluded outdoor patio located a roughly 15 minutes walk from the festival’s main center of gravity.

It was a rather sedate way to unveil what Dave Dugan, OpenAI’s head of global ads solutions, called “an entirely new ads product [and] an entirely new experience.”

“Why does someone open the ChatGPT app?” Dugan asked the (very sweaty) reporters taking notes in the 90-degree heat. “They want to do research, they want to solve a problem, they want to get information on a particular topic. They’re not coming to ChatGPT to scroll.”

It’s an interesting line coming from a longtime Meta executive, a company that helped define the art of stopping thumbs mid-scroll. Before joining OpenAI in April, Dugan spent more than 12 years at Meta, most recently as VP of global clients and agencies.

Speaking of Meta, it took them until 2021 – as in, 17 years – to break $100 billion in ad revenue. OpenAI, meanwhile, has reportedly told investors it expects to hit $100 billion in revenue within the next four years.

Whether that’s a realistic target is debatable. But here’s the pitch OpenAI is making to try and get there.

From attention to ‘intelligence’

Forget impressions and time spent. CRO Denise Dresser said OpenAI wants its advertising business to be measured by whether the ads help people get things done.

“We’re moving from the attention economy to the intelligence economy, and what consumers really want is usefulness,” she said. “And so that’s what we’re all about.”

Ads as an entrée

OpenAI also sees advertising not just as a revenue line but as a way to underwrite access to its product, especially for free users and those in lower-priced tiers.

“Our goal is to increase access for more people to better AI tools,” Dugan said. “As we build our ads platforms, it’s a way to subsidize those experiences and bring more information to more people. There’s a direct tie between ads and the mission of our business.”

For all intents and purchases

OpenAI now has more than 900 million weekly active users and around 20% of the questions people are asking have direct commercial intent, according to Dugan. But an even broader set of queries are upper funnel with commercial potential.

“Say, for instance, I’m planning a trip to the Alps with my family, and I ask ‘What’s a good time of the year to go?’” he said. “I’m not yet showing commercial intent yet, but that could be predictive of possibilities.”

Gotta have guardrails

Meanwhile, to make ads inside a chat feel acceptable to users, OpenAI is drawing bright lines, including clear ones around where sponsored messages appear and what stays off-limits to advertisers.

“We have to be very clear that we’re never sharing conversational information with advertisers,” Dugan said. “It’s an important topic for our users that we maintain that trust.”

Creative workflows

But what about the creative itself? We are in Cannes, after all, where it’s all about the work.

Well, the work is changing, said Chad Nelson, a creative specialist at OpenAI, because the scale of production is changing.

“I’ve gone around the world and talked to brands and they’re not producing assets in the thousands – they’re producing assets in the tens of thousands,” Nelson said. “Think about the languages, the different audiences, the different formats and the different platforms they have to publish on. It’s just a massive amount of work to create, and I think that’s where OpenAI and our models can play a huge role.”

No coding experience required

The interesting part isn’t just having more tools, though, Nelson added; it’s about being able to build your own, even if you don’t know how to write code.

Using Codex, which is OpenAI’s coding agent, a creative director can sketch out a workflow in natural language and pretty easily turn it into a working app, he said.

“I don’t code – I actually don’t code at all – but I know how to talk to these systems,” Nelson said. “Some of the best creative directors in your company can now become R&D leaders; they can actually start to design and think about production workflows, tools and systems.”

Live to Palais another day

But do creatives want to become R&D leaders? Someone should walk over the Palais where they’re getting their Lions Awards and ask them.

Nelson pushed back, however, on the notion that AI will squeeze agencies out of the picture.

“This is where it gets very complementary,” he said. “I’ve talked to brands and I’ve talked to their agencies, as well, and ultimately it goes back to the sheer quantity of assets that need to be produced. If I can [do that] in a way that becomes more effective and talk to people on a more personal level – I think that’s what both brands and agencies want.”

Big baby steps

Yet for all its ambition, OpenAI is also at pains to stress that its ads business is still in its infancy.

“We’re still very early in this – today is 19 weeks since we launched this ads product,” Dugan said. “It’s like a baby; for a while, you talk about how old your baby is in weeks.”

But things are moving fast.

Since February, OpenAI has launched its ads pilot in the US; rolled out an ad manager in beta; added international markets, including the UK and Australia; released conversion tracking; struck partnerships with ad tech companies, agencies and brands; and went from selling ads only on CPM basis to also offering a cost-per-click option, which now accounts for the majority of spend on the platform.

“We are clearly in the advertising business now,” Dresser said.

title: Berlin Reiterates Its No to UniCredit's Exchange Offer for Commerzbank | MarketScreener
description:
(Alliance News) - The German government is once again opposing UniCredit's bid for Commerzbank as the public exchange offer reopens, Milano Finanza reported Tuesday.
According to government sources, Berlin does not intend to tender into the offer or sell its 13% stake, preserving its position as the second-largest shareholder.
At the end of the first phase of the offer, UniCredit held 39.18% of Commerzbank.
As the newspaper reports, Berlin reiterated that Commerzbank's independence is the best solution for the German economy, arguing that UniCredit's offer does not provide an adequate premium to shareholders and calling the Italian group's approach "aggressive".
Among the objections is the use of derivatives to build the stake in Commerzbank, while the exchange ratio on offer was, for much of the acceptance period, less attractive than selling the shares on the market.
text:
(Alliance News) - The German government is once again opposing UniCredit's bid for Commerzbank as the public exchange offer reopens, Milano Finanza reported Tuesday.

According to government sources, Berlin does not intend to tender into the offer or sell its 13% stake, preserving its position as the second-largest shareholder.

At the end of the first phase of the offer, UniCredit held 39.18% of Commerzbank. Including derivatives positions, the total stake rises to 55.6%, a level that, once regulatory approvals are secured and the position is converted into shares, would allow the Italian group to take control of the bank's governance.

As the newspaper reports, Berlin reiterated that Commerzbank's independence is the best solution for the German economy, arguing that UniCredit's offer does not provide an adequate premium to shareholders and calling the Italian group's approach "aggressive".

Among the objections is the use of derivatives to build the stake in Commerzbank, while the exchange ratio on offer was, for much of the acceptance period, less attractive than selling the shares on the market.

June 22 (Reuters) - IBM on Monday said it has partnered with OpenAI to integrate frontier AI capabilities into enterprise security workflows, aiming to counter rapidly evolving cyber threats.

Shares of the company rose 3.6% in trading after the bell.

Here are a few details on the partnership:

o IBM joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program and is collaborating with the startup to integrate protective AI tools directly into business operations, helping companies identify and minimize their security risks.

o As part of the partnership, the company launched a new application security service that uses OpenAI's cyber capabilities to help organizations identify and validate software vulnerabilities with greater speed and precision.

o The new service is built on Project Lightwell, an initiative launched last month to deploy engineers and AI tools to help companies better secure open source software and is backed by a $5 billion commitment from IBM and Red Hat.

o Project Lightwell will use OpenAI's cyber capabilities alongside other frontier AI models for code review and remediation.

o "The OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program expands our access to a broader set of advanced AI capabilities, which we deploy within our clients' environments to help surface the most relevant risks faster and help them act with confidence," said Mark Hughes, global managing partner, cybersecurity services, IBM Consulting.

text:
A lawsuit led by a Detroit pension fund accuses Uber management and its board of putting profits ahead of compliance and safety, decisions that have exposed the company and its shareholders to risk.

The lawsuit, which was filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California in San Francisco, alleges that Uber is a “serial compliance offender” that has “knowingly” cut corners. This lack of compliance culture has led to thousands of lawsuits by victims who have alleged sexual assault and harassment by drivers, according to the complaint.

The lawsuit, which names CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, claims board members breached their fiduciary duty to the company and its shareholders by ignoring repeated warnings of compliance and safety failures. The plaintiffs want Uber’s leaders to personally compensate the company for alleged harm, return certain compensation they received, and implement stronger oversight and compliance measures.

“The victims of this lack of compliance culture include sexual assault and harassment victims, customers with disabilities, and unwary consumers looking to subscribe to Uber One,” the complaint reads.

Uber pushed back on the accusations in the lawsuit.

“This suit ignores important facts and is based on misleading, false narratives from other meritless lawsuits that we have already addressed publicly and in the courtroom,” an Uber spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.

It’s not unusual for companies like Uber to face derivative lawsuits, when a shareholder sues the company’s directors on behalf of the corporation. Shareholders have filed such lawsuits against Adobe, Apple, and Intel this year, for instance.
